conceptTag: Return on investment for the customer
readerTitle: The pricier bid won. It did the customer's math.
caseNote: 가상 사례 (제빵 공장에 입찰한 설비 유지보수 업체 두 곳, 단열 시공업체와 집주인) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 기업 고객은 가격이 아니라 자기 숫자로 계산한 회수액을 산다. 판매자의 일은 그 계산을 고객과 함께, 믿을 수 있게 해 주는 것이다.
misconception: 더 싸게 부르거나 기능을 더 많이 나열하면 이긴다. 투자수익률은 판매자가 크게 말할수록 설득력이 커진다.

sources.text: 재무의 표준 개념 (투자수익률 ROI, 투자 회수 기간)

factChecks.note: 단열 시공 계산: 공사비 $4,800 ÷ 연 절감액 $960 = 회수 기간 5년. 연 $960은 집주인의 지난 고지서를 근거로 한다는 가정의 가상 수치이며, 실제 절감액은 집, 기후, 에너지 가격에 따라 크게 다릅니다. 실제 절감률은 카드에 쓰지 않았습니다.
소프트웨어 노트의 '절약한 시간은 다른 일에 쓰일 때만 이익'이라는 주장은 일반 원리로만 서술했고 특정 연구 수치를 인용하지 않았습니다.

cards.title: The pricier bid won. It did the customer's math.
body: Two maintenance firms bid to look after the ovens and mixers at a mid-sized bakery. Firm A asked $2,000 a month. Firm B asked $3,000.
The bakery owner picked Firm B. She wasn't being generous. Firm B had shown her a number from her own business that Firm A never asked about.

image.label: Two proposals on a bakery office desk, one with a simple calculation circled
image.brief: 제빵 공장 사무실 책상 위에 제안서 두 장. 왼쪽은 기능 목록이 빽빽한 제안서("$2,000/mo"), 오른쪽은 짧은 계산식에 동그라미가 쳐진 제안서("$3,000/mo"). 뒤 창문 너머로 오븐 라인. 실제 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You're 50% more expensive. How do you pitch?
body: You run Firm B. Your plan includes scheduled checks that catch worn parts before they break. Firm A only comes when something fails.
The owner says, "Your price is a lot higher." What do you do next?

options.text: Drop your price closer to $2,000 to stay in the race
options.feedback: You may win the contract, but you give away the margin that pays for the scheduled checks. And you still haven't shown why your plan is worth more.

options.text: Send a longer list of your services and certifications
options.feedback: It proves you are capable. It leaves her to work out what that capability is worth in dollars, and most buyers won't.

options.text: Ask what an hour of stopped production costs her, then work out the gain together
options.feedback: You move the talk from your price to her return. It takes more effort, and it only works if your claim holds up against her own numbers.

cards.title: The bakery's numbers, not the firm's.
body: Every extra $1 the bakery spends brings back about **$6**. Firm A was cheaper. Firm B was the better deal.

breakdown.label: Cost of one hour stopped
breakdown.detail: Lost output, idle staff, wasted dough

breakdown.label: Downtime saved per month
breakdown.detail: Estimated from the bakery's own repair log

cards.title: Return on investment for the customer
body: **Return on investment (ROI)** compares what a customer gets back with what they pay. For a business buyer, a purchase is an investment. It has to earn more than it costs.
Firm A sold maintenance. Firm B sold fewer stopped ovens, priced in the owner's own dollars. The owner could also take that number to her partner and defend the choice.

image.label: A scale: $1,000 extra cost on one side, $6,000 gain on the other
image.brief: 단순한 저울 일러스트. 왼쪽 접시에 작은 동전 더미 "Extra cost $1,000", 오른쪽 접시에 큰 더미 "Gain $6,000". 오른쪽이 확실히 아래로 기움. 플랫한 인포그래픽 스타일.

cards.title: Three numbers, all from the customer.
body: A believable customer ROI rests on three numbers. Each one should come from the customer's records, not your brochure.
list: **Gain:** money earned, saved or protected (output, hours, mistakes, risk)
**Cost:** everything they pay, not just your price
**Time:** how long until the gain covers the cost, called the *payback period*
cards.callout: Ask questions first. Calculate second. Pitch last.
cards.softwareNote: Software ROI is often pitched as "hours saved × hourly wage." Saved hours only count if people spend them on work that earns or saves money. Ask what the team will do with that time.

cards.title: The return has to reach the person who pays.
body: Suppose the bakery's maintenance manager holds the budget, but the gain shows up in production numbers. He sees a cost of $1,000 more. The gain is on someone else's report.
A strong ROI can still lose if it lands in the wrong place. Show each person in the decision where the return appears for them.

cards.title: Big claims get discounted.
body: Buyers know sellers want the deal, so they shrink any ROI a seller brings. An inflated claim costs you trust that is hard to win back.

Use conservative estimates and give a range, not a promise. If the return depends on the customer changing how they work, say so. And don't ignore what a spreadsheet misses: comfort, calm and fewer late-night emergencies matter too.

cards.title: Now it's home insulation.
body: You insulate homes. A job costs $4,800. Based on the homeowner's last year of heating bills, you estimate savings of about $960 a year.
She says, "That's a lot of money." What do you say?

image.label: A house cutaway with heat escaping through the roof
image.brief: 집 단면도 일러스트. 지붕과 벽으로 빨간 열 화살표가 새어 나가고, 옆에 난방비 고지서 한 장. 따뜻한 색감. 실제 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

options.text: Offer 15% off if she signs this week
options.feedback: A discount shortens her payback a little and may close the sale. It also teaches her your price was soft, without showing what she actually gets back.

options.text: Show the math from her own bills: about 5 years to pay back, then savings each year after, plus a warmer house
options.feedback: She can check every number herself, so she trusts it. Five years is a slower answer than she might hope for, but it is one she can believe.

options.text: Tell her it usually pays for itself within a year
options.feedback: It sounds great today. When her bills don't match, you lose her referral and maybe a review.

cards.title: Sell the return, in the customer's own numbers.
body: Business customers don't buy your price. They buy what they get back for it. Help them calculate it honestly, with their data.
**Try it today:** pick one customer. Write down what your product saves or earns them each month, and how long until it covers what they pay.
